name: Penicillin (1928)
teaser: Alexander Fleming left a window open over a Petri dish on vacation. By the time he came back, a mold had killed every bacterium in the dish — the most consequential accident of the 20th century.

exploreAction.targetName: Howard Florey & Ernst Chain's 1940 paper on penicillin
exploreAction.instruction: It's a short medical paper with eleven authors. Read the first paragraph and the last: between them is the most cited clinical trial of the early 20th century. Then look at the references — half of the most cited papers in medicine are referenced just in this paper.

name: DNA Double Helix (1953)
teaser: Watson and Crick solved the structure of life from a card table without doing an experiment. The data came from Rosalind Franklin's X-ray photograph, taken in a King's College hallway by a student who did not get the credit.

exploreAction.targetName: Watson & Crick's 1953 Nature paper, "A Structure for Deoxyribose Nucleic Acid" (one page)
exploreAction.instruction: It's just one page. It is the single most cited paper in biology. Read the second paragraph — "It has not escaped our notice..." — and see what the famous undertone is. Then read the citation to Franklin's unpublished work and ask why.

name: Gravitational Waves (2015)
teaser: Einstein predicted them in 1916 and wrote that he'd bet a year of his life we'd never detect them. 99 years and $1B later, an instrument in Louisiana heard two black holes collide.

exploreAction.targetName: LIGO's 2016 detection paper (Phys. Rev. Lett.)
exploreAction.instruction: Notice the data plots on page 2. The signal is visible to your eye — a 0.2-second chirp rising in frequency. Then read the timing: the signal was detected 7 milliseconds before the Louisiana detector and the Washington detector independently confirmed it.

name: Higgs Boson (2012)
teaser: A theoretical particle proposed in 1964 to explain why matter has mass, then sought by 30,000 physicists for 48 years and finally confirmed at the LHC on July 4, 2012.

exploreAction.targetName: CMS + ATLAS simultaneous 2012 announcement papers
exploreAction.instruction: Read the abstract of both papers. They give a 5-sigma confidence — that's a 1 in 3.4 million chance the signal is noise. Then read the figures: each dot in the chart is one particle collision, and the bump at 125 GeV is the Higgs.

name: Special and General Relativity (1905, 1915)
teaser: Einstein at 26 wrote four papers in 1905 that broke time, mass, and energy apart and patched them back together. Ten years later he added gravity as geometry.

exploreAction.targetName: Einstein's 1905 paper "On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies" — first 4 pages
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first four pages. Then skip to the end. The middle is the math, which is intimidating, but the argue in plain language up front. The famous E = mc² is in part 5 of a follow-up paper later that year — a throwaway bonus in a paper on something else.

name: Quantum Mechanics (1925–27)
teaser: Six European physicists in three years invented a new kind of physics where particles are also waves and measurements change the thing being measured. None of them finished the work, all of them were right.

exploreAction.targetName: Heisenberg's 1927 paper "Über den anschaulichen Inhalt der quantentheoretischen Kinematik und Mechanik"
exploreAction.instruction: It's 27 pages. The famous uncertainty principle is at the bottom of page 3 of a footnote. Read it. Then notice the phrasing — Heisenberg is offended by his own conclusion, not triumphant.

name: Evolution by Natural Selection (1858)
teaser: Two Englishmen and a Malay archipelago letter exchange published the same idea on the same day — Darwin and Wallace — and Darwin got the credit because he'd been working on it longer.

exploreAction.targetName: Darwin & Wallace, 1858 Linnean Society joint presentation (transcript)
exploreAction.instruction: It's two papers side by side. Read Wallace's first. Read Darwin's second. They say almost exactly the same thing in different dialects. That the same theory appeared twice in different minds is itself the proof of evolution.

name: Periodic Table (1869)
teaser: Mendeleev arranged the known elements on a card table in two weeks, then realized the gaps he'd left unfilled predicted eight elements that hadn't been discovered yet.

exploreAction.targetName: Mendeleev's 1869 paper "On the Relation between the Properties and Atomic Weights of the Elements"
exploreAction.instruction: It's four pages. Read the table. The empty cells are not laziness — they're predictions. Read the sentence about 'eka-silicon.' That element was discovered 17 years later and called germanium, exactly where Mendeleev said it would be.

name: Photosynthesis (1770s–1800s)
teaser: Joseph Priestley burned a candle in a sealed jar, then put mint in; the mint resurrected the air. He had no idea he'd found the only thing keeping animals alive.

exploreAction.targetName: Jan Ingenhousz's 1779 paper "Experiments upon Vegetables"
exploreAction.instruction: Most of it is botanical observation. Read carefully for the moment where he describes that plants only "restore" air in light, not in darkness. That single observation tells you plants are doing light-driven chemistry — which is exactly photosynthesis.

name: Radioactivity (1896)
teaser: Becquerel put uranium salts in a drawer next to photographic plates. When he developed the plates he found fog — and that fog was energy that no chemistry of the time could explain.

exploreAction.targetName: Marie Curie's 1898 paper "Rays emitted by uranium and thorium compounds"
exploreAction.instruction: She uses the word "radioactivity" for the first time in history. Read the closing paragraph where she suggests the rays are an atomic phenomenon. She was right, and the term stuck.

name: Germ Theory of Disease (1860s–80s)
teaser: Pasteur, Koch and Lister transformed medicine by proving most disease came from microorganisms — and that washing your hands with soap was a cure.

exploreAction.targetName: Pasteur's 1861 paper "On the organized bodies which exist in the atmosphere"
exploreAction.instruction: It's a public lecture — Pasteur wrote it as a lecture because no journal would publish his experiments at the time. Read the part where he boils broth in swan-necked flasks. The flask alone disproves spontaneous generation.

name: Big Bang Cosmology (1927)
teaser: Lemaître reasoned backward from Einstein's equations to a single point of origin — and Einstein told him his math was wrong before relenting 12 years later.

exploreAction.targetName: Lemaître's 1927 paper "A homogeneous universe of constant mass and increasing radius" (English translation)
exploreAction.instruction: It's 7 pages. The conclusion is hidden in plain text — there's no fanfare. He writes: "We may conceive of the beginning of the universe in the form of a unique atom." Then asks if it was. The answer of "yes" arrived in 1964.

name: Cosmic Microwave Background (1964)
teaser: Two Bell Labs engineers trying to calibrate a radio antenna heard a low hiss that wouldn't go away. They spent a year ruling out pigeon droppings before publishing.

exploreAction.targetName: Penzias and Wilson's 1965 paper "A Measurement of Excess Antenna Temperature at 4080 Mc/s"
exploreAction.instruction: Two pages. There is no cosmology in it. It's an antenna temperature paper. Read the appendix — there's a footnote about 'dielectric bird excreta'. The Nobel committee cited them anyway because that hiss turned out to be the universe at age 380,000 years.

name: Plate Tectonics (1960s)
teaser: A handful of oceanographers and geophysicists noticed mid-ocean ridges and matching coastlines in the 1950s, refused to give up on a ridiculed theory for a decade, then reshaped geology.

exploreAction.targetName: Tuzo Wilson's 1965 paper "A new class of faults and their bearing on continental drift"
exploreAction.instruction: It's only 7 pages. Read the third figure. Wilson proposes transform faults simply by looking at a seafloor map. The whole field hesitates for another 3 years before agreeing; in those 3 years, every geology textbook in the world is rewritten.

name: Calculus (1665–1676)
teaser: Newton invented it during the plague years in his Lincolnshire home. Leibniz published it first. The two became Europe's longest-running scientific argument.

exploreAction.targetName: Leibniz's 1684 paper "Nova Methodus pro Maximis et Minimis" (Latin translated)
exploreAction.instruction: It's six pages. The first paragraph explains the entire theory. He uses dx and dy for the first time. Then read how Newton deferred — published his version years later with the same notation we still use.

name: Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems (1931)
teaser: Austrian mathematician working alone in Vienna proved that any arithmetic system rich enough to be useful is also rich enough to be inconsistent. Hilbert said it couldn't be done.

exploreAction.targetName: Gödel's 1931 paper "Über formal unentscheidbare Sätze der Principia Mathematica"
exploreAction.instruction: It's dense. Don't try to follow the proof. Read the introduction — he lists the previous assumptions carefully. Then look at the page where he writes 'Satz XI' and understand that's the heart of his finding. The result is anyway intuitively graspable: any formal system...

name: Transistor (1947)
teaser: Bell Labs physicists trying to make a better amplifier accidentally invented the device that gave us every computer since, then won the Nobel six years later.

exploreAction.targetName: Bardeen, Brattain, and Shockley's 1948 papers in Phys. Rev.
exploreAction.instruction: Read Bardeen & Brattain's 1948 paper first. It's a two-page experimental note. Then Shockley's — he had tried to suppress it, then published his own theory three days later. Between them is the entire history of the patent dispute that runs to 1956.

name: Integrated Circuit (1959)
teaser: Kilby at Texas Instruments put two transistors on one germanium sliver by hand, then filed a patent six months before Noyce at Fairchild did the same thing with silicon.

exploreAction.targetName: Kilby's 1959 patent (US 3,138,743)
exploreAction.instruction: It's a patent, so the language islegalistic. Read the first figure — hand-drawn from 1959. Then read the second figure and the third. By claim 4, you've seen what every chip in your phone still resembles.

name: Laser (1960)
teaser: Theoretically predicted by Einstein in 1917, the first working laser was built by Maiman in 1960 from a ruby rod, a flashlamp, and the insight that pink rubies could amplify light.

exploreAction.targetName: Maiman's 1960 paper "Stimulated Optical Radiation in Ruby" (Nature)
exploreAction.instruction: Two pages. Maiman was told by theorists the ruby would never work. The paper shows otherwise. Then read the editor's note — he had to fight Nature twice to get it published.

name: Internet (ARPANET, 1969)
teaser: Four US university computers sent the first packet on October 29, 1969. The intended message was "LOGIN." The first two letters got through before the system crashed.

exploreAction.targetName: Cerf's 1974 paper "A Protocol for Packet Network Intercommunication"
exploreAction.instruction: It's a clear 26-page paper. Read the introduction for why you need TCP. Then look at the figures. The diagrams of "TCP headers" still describe the spirit of every packet on your phone.

name: World Wide Web (1989)
teaser: CERN physicist Tim Berners-Lee proposed a global hypertext system on a notepad in March 1989. He built the first browser and server by Christmas.

exploreAction.targetName: Berners-Lee's 1989 proposal, "Information Management: A Proposal"
exploreAction.instruction: It's two pages. Written as a memo to his manager at CERN. The phrase 'vague but exciting' is the boss's margin note. Read the remaining figure of the network diagram — it's a child of the 80s and it became the web we use every day.

name: CRISPR Gene Editing (2012)
teaser: Doudna and Charpentier figured out that bacteria were using a piece of viral RNA as a programmable knife. Five years later it won the Nobel.

exploreAction.targetName: Jinek et al., 2012 paper "A programmable dual-RNA-guided DNA endonuclease in adaptive bacterial immunity" (Science)
exploreAction.instruction: It's six pages. Read the first figure. It's a cartoon of two RNA molecules finding a strand of DNA — and cutting it. Then read the conclusion. The first time a human sits down to read it, they understand the future of biology changed in 2012.

name: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (1977)
teaser: Lauterbur took a snapshot of two test tubes of water inside a magnet by varying the magnetic field, and got the first MRI image. The hospital where he worked then refused to file the patent.

exploreAction.targetName: Lauterbur's 1973 paper "Image Formation by Induced Local Interactions: Examples Employing Nuclear Magnetic Resonance" (Nature)
exploreAction.instruction: One page. Read the second figure — it's a fuzzy image of two tubes. That image is the one that made Lauterbur realize you could see inside a body without X-rays.

name: Helicobacter pylori (1982)
teaser: Australian pathologist Barry Marshall drank a flask of bacteria to prove ulcers were caused by infection, not stress. He and his partner won the 2005 Nobel.

exploreAction.targetName: Marshall & Warren's 1984 paper "Unidentified curved bacilli in the stomach of patients with gastritis and peptic ulceration" (Lancet)
exploreAction.instruction: It's a 9-page clinical note. Read the patient descriptions on the third page. Then read the closing — Marshall says he'll now treat patients with antibiotics and see. The next year he tests himself by drinking the bacterium, getting gastritis, and curing himself with...

name: Control of Fire (~1 million years ago)
teaser: Pre-homo erectus hominids at Wonderwerk Cave, South Africa, left the earliest known ash layer from a controlled fire 1.5M years ago — the first time anything on Earth burned on purpose.

exploreAction.targetName: Berna et al., 2012 paper "Early use of controlled fire in Wonderwerk Cave, South Africa" (PNAS)
exploreAction.instruction: Read the figures. The ash layers are 20cm deep, with bone tools at the same level. Read the dating method — they used micromagnetostratigraphy because the sediments were too old for radiocarbon. The age is contested but the fire isn't.

name: Wheel (~3500 BCE)
teaser: Mesopotamian potters who had already invented the turntable also invented wheels for transport within a few centuries — then it took another thousand years to bolt the two together and make the chariot.

exploreAction.targetName: Vorderasiatisches Museum Berlin (Mesopotamian collection)
exploreAction.instruction: Zero in on the wheel-shaped clay tokens from the Uruk period (~4000 BCE). They're not transport — they're counters. The first 'wheel' was a step in writing; the second was for transport. The order is what makes this hard to believe.

name: Printing Press (c. 1440)
teaser: Johannes Gutenberg invented the movable-type printing press in Mainz, and within 50 years there were 20M books in Europe — more than all the scribes of the previous millennium combined.

exploreAction.targetName: Gutenberg Museum, Mainz
exploreAction.instruction: Turn to the two-page Gutenberg Bible on display. Each letter was hand-set, hand-inked, hand-pressed. The shop could produce 250 pages a day. Now try to imagine being a 1455 reader seeing one for the first time — the world had no reference for moving text.

name: Lightning is Electricity (1752)
teaser: Benjamin Franklin flew a kite in a thunderstorm, with a metal key tied to the string. The key sparked. The entire scientific community decided not to repeat the experiment.

exploreAction.targetName: Franklin's 1751 letter to Peter Collinson on electrical experiments
exploreAction.instruction: It's a popular-audience letter, so it reads well. Read the second paragraph — he proposes the experiment. He never writes that he did it himself; only that the experiment was performed. We're not even sure he flew the kite.

name: Streptomycin (1943)
teaser: Waksman's graduate student Albert Schatz isolated streptomycin from a soil sample in 1943. Waksman took the patent credit. Schatz sued and eventually won a settlement.

exploreAction.instruction: Two-page paper. The first author is Schatz — the graduate student. The third is Waksman, who took the patent credit. The medical import is in the last paragraph: it works against the tuberculosis bacillus.
exploreAction.targetName: Schatz, Bugie, and Waksman, 1944 paper (Proc. Soc. Exp. Biol. Med.)

name: Antiseptic Surgery (1867)
teaser: Joseph Lister read Pasteur's germ theory papers and decided that the secret to saving surgical patients was washing everything in carbolic acid — including the surgeons' hands.

exploreAction.targetName: Lister's 1867 paper "On the Antiseptic Principle in the Practice of Surgery" (Lancet)
exploreAction.instruction: Read the before-and-after hospital ward mortality numbers in table 1. The amputation ward mortality went from near-50% to near-zero. That's a 50% statistical effect on a working hospital ward, with no drugs involved. Just washing.

name: Mendel's Laws of Inheritance (1865)
teaser: An Austrian monk bred 29,000 pea plants in his monastery garden, articulated the math of inherited traits in 1865, then died before anyone in the scientific community paid attention.

exploreAction.targetName: Mendel's 1865 paper "Versuche über Pflanzenhybriden" (trans. Experiments on Plant Hybrids)
exploreAction.instruction: Mendel presents the ratio 3:1 in F2 pea plants. Read that table. It's the foundation of genetics. Then notice that 'gen' isn't named in the paper — he called them 'factors.' The terms came later.

name: Oxygen and Combustion Chemistry (1770s)
teaser: Lavoisier weighed everything. He weighed water before and after burning it through a gun barrel, and showed it gained mass — and weighed the air that lost it — and chemistry was born.

exploreAction.targetName: Lavoisier, 1789 "Traité Élémentaire de Chimie" — first chapter
exploreAction.instruction: It reads like a textbook chapter. Read the part where he describes 'oxygen' for the first time. He renamed it 'oxygène' — 'acid-former.' His previous term was 'deflogisticated air.' Within a generation, chemistry textbooks globally dropped the old language.

name: Viviani's Theorem (1659)
teaser: Italian mathematician who computed the area of a partial sphere's surface by balancing a cube against the curve of a half-circle.

exploreAction.targetName: Viviani's letters to Leibniz and Michelangelo Ricci (1659)
exploreAction.instruction: The letters are mostly in Italian and short. Read the one to Leibniz — it describes the theorem in two pages. Now draw what he describes on a piece of paper. The proof you see in two minutes took him weeks; that's the difference between writing and re-discovering...

name: Fibonacci / Hindu-Arabic Numerals in Europe (1202)
teaser: Leonardo of Pisa spent his childhood in North African markets, brought Hindu-Arabic numerals back to Europe in 1202, and changed how the world does arithmetic.

exploreAction.targetName: Fibonacci's "Liber Abaci" — opening chapter
exploreAction.instruction: European merchants in 1202 still used Roman numerals. They couldn't do real arithmetic. Read the first three pages of Liber Abaci — Fibonacci explains why 'IX × IX' as Roman arithmetic is harder than '9 × 9' as positional arithmetic.

name: Atomic Nucleus / Proton (1911)
teaser: Rutherford fired alpha particles at gold foil in his Manchester lab. He expected them to pass through. A few bounced back. His assistant Marsden reportedly said it was like firing a 15-inch shell at tissue paper and having it come back.

exploreAction.targetName: Rutherford, 1911 paper "The Scattering of α and β Particles by Matter and the Structure of the Atom" (Phil. Mag.)
exploreAction.instruction: It's seven pages. Read the opening — he lists what he expected to find. Then read the conclusion. He tells you the atom has a 'central charge' almost the whole mass of the atom concentrated in a tiny region. Today we call it the nucleus.

name: The Cosmic Microwave Background (1965)
teaser: In 1964, two Bell Labs engineers pointed a horn antenna at the sky to test satellite communications and heard a hiss that wouldn't go away — even after they cleaned pigeon droppings out of the horn. The hiss was the afterglow of the Big Bang, cooling for 13.8 billion years, and it had been predicted by theory just 16 years earlier.

exploreAction.targetName: The cosmic microwave background — Penzias & Wilson's 1964 hiss
exploreAction.instruction: Read how the discovery worked: the universe's first light, released 380,000 years after the Big Bang, has stretched from white-hot to microwave wavelengths by the expansion of space — about 3 degrees above absolute zero. Penzias and Wilson had no idea what the hiss was; they spent months eliminating every earthly source, and only learned it was the 'primordial fireball' when a Princeton physicist heard about their problem.

name: Exoplanets (1995)
teaser: For centuries astronomers assumed other stars had planets, but no one could see one — then in 1995 two Swiss astronomers found a planet orbiting the star 51 Pegasi by watching the star wobble. The planet was a 'hot Jupiter,' a gas giant orbiting closer than Mercury, and it rewrote every theory of how solar systems form.

exploreAction.targetName: 51 Pegasi b — the first confirmed exoplanet (1995)
exploreAction.instruction: Understand the method first: a planet's gravity tugs its star, and that wobble shifts the star's light slightly red then blue — the radial velocity method. Mayor and Queloz detected a 4-day wobble in 51 Pegasi, meaning a planet 150 times Earth's mass orbiting far too close to its star to exist by the old rules.

name: Evolution by Natural Selection (1859)
teaser: Darwin's On the Origin of Species (1859) — 1,250 copies sold out on the first day — proposed that species change by natural selection: variation, inheritance, and differential survival. He spent two decades hesitating to publish, and the theory's famous phrase, 'survival of the fittest,' was actually coined by Herbert Spencer, not Darwin.

exploreAction.targetName: On the Origin of Species (1859) — chapters 1 and 4
exploreAction.instruction: Read the Origin's introduction and the final paragraph — Darwin's summary, including the overlooked line that selection works on 'domestic productions' and nature alike. Then read chapter 4's pigeon-breeding analogy: Darwin leaned on breeders' experience because, as he admits, the fossil record of his time showed 'no finely graduated organic chain.'

name: The Periodic Table (1869)
teaser: Dmitri Mendeleev published his periodic table in 1869, arranging the 63 known elements by atomic weight — and leaving deliberate gaps for elements that didn't exist yet, predicting gallium, scandium, and germanium to within striking accuracy. He reportedly saw the table in a dream after three days of exhaustion.

exploreAction.targetName: Mendeleev's 1869 periodic table vs. the modern one
exploreAction.instruction: Look at Mendeleev's 1869 original table and compare it with the modern one: his rows and columns don't match today's because he ordered by atomic weight, not atomic number. Then find the three predicted elements (eka-aluminum, eka-boron, eka-silicon) and check their properties against Mendeleev's predictions — the germanium match is almost embarrassing in its accuracy.

name: Radiocarbon Dating (1949)
teaser: Willard Libby's radiocarbon dating, announced in 1949, measures the decay of carbon-14 (half-life ~5,730 years) to date organic remains up to ~50,000 years old. He proved it worked by dating Egyptian artifacts whose ages were already known — and the technique immediately rewrote archaeology, from the Dead Sea Scrolls to Ötzi the Iceman.

exploreAction.targetName: Libby's 1949 Science paper — the Egyptian artifact validation
exploreAction.instruction: Read the 1949 paper's validation: Libby dated wood from a First Dynasty Egyptian tomb and got within a century of the accepted age, which is what convinced the field. Then understand the calibration problem: atmospheric carbon-14 varies over time (nuclear testing changed it), so raw dates must be calibrated against tree rings — which is why radiocarbon ages carry the 'BP' (before present) notation.

name: The Polio Vaccine (1955)
teaser: Jonas Salk's inactivated polio vaccine was declared safe on 12 April 1955 — the same day the field trial of 1.8 million children was announced as a success, making Salk an overnight national hero. Asked who owned the patent, he answered: 'Well, the people, I would say. There is no patent. Could you patent the sun?'.

exploreAction.targetName: The 12 April 1955 announcement + the Cutter Incident
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the 1955 announcement newsreel and notice the scale: the field trial was the largest medical experiment in history at the time. Then read about the Cutter Incident, weeks later, when a faulty batch of vaccine paralyzed 200 children — the response created the modern vaccine-safety regulatory system, which is the trial's real legacy.

name: The First Organ Transplant (1954)
teaser: On 23 December 1954, surgeon Joseph Murray transplanted a kidney from Ronald Herrick into his identical twin brother Richard at Boston's Peter Bent Brigham Hospital — the first successful organ transplant in history. It worked precisely because the twins were genetically identical, which sidestepped the immune rejection that had killed all previous attempts.

exploreAction.targetName: The 1954 Herrick case report + Murray's 1990 Nobel lecture
exploreAction.instruction: Read the 1954 case report and notice what it concedes: the transplant 'merely' moved a kidney between genetically identical bodies, so no immunosuppression was needed. Then read the longer arc — the development of immunosuppressive drugs (azathioprine, then cyclosporine) that made transplants between unrelated people possible, for which Murray won the 1990 Nobel.

name: CT Scanning (1971)
teaser: The first CT scan of a patient's head was performed in October 1971 at Atkinson Morley Hospital in London — the machine, built by engineer Godfrey Hounsfield, took 160 parallel readings and required a room-sized computer to assemble the image. Hounsfield shared the 1979 Nobel in Physiology or Medicine.

exploreAction.targetName: The 1971 first CT image vs. a modern head scan
exploreAction.instruction: Start with the first CT image — a cyst in a woman's brain, rendered as a grid of numbers — and compare it with a modern scan: the improvement is in resolution, not principle. Then read how the machine worked: an X-ray source rotated around the head taking slice-by-slice readings, and a computer solved the equations to reconstruct the slice, an idea Hounsfield had while wondering how to map the contents of a box without opening it.

name: Stem Cells (1998)
teaser: James Thomson isolated the first human embryonic stem cells in 1998 at the University of Wisconsin — cells that can become any tissue in the body. The announcement ignited a research and ethics firestorm that shaped American politics for a decade, with some states funding the work and the federal government restricting it.

exploreAction.targetName: Thomson's 1998 Science paper + the ethics timeline
exploreAction.instruction: Read the 1998 Science paper's restrained opening, then look at the timeline it set: Thomson grew the cells for months and showed they could differentiate into the three germ layers. Then read how the field evolved around the political fight — induced pluripotent stem cells (2006) were developed partly as an ethical end-run around the embryo debate.

name: Induced Pluripotent Stem Cells (2006)
teaser: Shinya Yamanaka announced in 2006 that he had turned adult mouse skin cells back into embryonic-like stem cells using just four genes (Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, c-Myc) — the 'iPS' cell, a Nobel Prize in 2012. The discovery made the embryo debate moot overnight, because the starting material was ordinary adult tissue.

exploreAction.targetName: Yamanaka's 2006 Cell paper — the four-factor screen
exploreAction.instruction: Read Yamanaka's 2006 Cell paper and notice the scale of the effort: he screened 24 candidate genes and found the combination of four that worked, an approach colleagues called reckless until it worked. Then follow the 'Yamanaka factors' into the clinic: patient-specific iPS cells are now used to model diseases and, increasingly, to build transplant tissue.

name: The First Exoplanet (1992)
teaser: The first confirmed planets outside our solar system were announced in 1992 — not around a sun-like star, but orbiting a pulsar, the crushed corpse of a dead star, found by Aleksander Wolszczan and Dale Frail. Three years later, 51 Pegasi b became the first planet found around a normal star, earning Mayor and Queloz the 2019 Nobel.

exploreAction.targetName: The 1992 pulsar planets paper + the 51 Pegasi b discovery
exploreAction.instruction: Read the 1992 discovery and notice why the pulsar planets were so hard to believe: the timing anomalies of the pulsar's radio pulses are exquisitely regular, and the planets were inferred from their gravitational tug. Then read about 51 Pegasi b — a 'hot Jupiter' so close to its star that it orbits in four days, which broke every theory of how planets form.

name: The Accelerating Universe (1998)
teaser: In 1998 two rival teams — one led by Saul Perlmutter, the other by Brian Schmidt and Adam Riess — independently found that distant supernovae were dimmer than expected: the universe's expansion is accelerating, pushed by an unknown 'dark energy' that makes up about 68% of everything. It won the 2011 Nobel and rewrote cosmology.

exploreAction.targetName: The 1998 Perlmutter and Riess–Schmidt supernova papers
exploreAction.instruction: Read how the measurement works: Type Ia supernovae explode with a known peak brightness, so their apparent dimness measures distance — and the 1998 data showed distant ones were farther than their redshift implied. Then read the discovery papers' own surprise: both teams expected to measure deceleration, and both published evidence of acceleration with visible reluctance.

name: The God Particle (2012)
teaser: On 4 July 2012, CERN announced the discovery of the Higgs boson — the particle predicted in 1964 that gives other particles mass — after a 48-year search at the Large Hadron Collider. The nickname 'God particle' was coined by Nobel laureate Leon Lederman, who reportedly wanted to call it the 'goddamn particle.'.

exploreAction.targetName: The 4 July 2012 CERN announcement — the Higgs bump plots
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the 4 July 2012 announcement video and look at the actual data: the Higgs appears as a small bump over background in the invariant-mass plots, and physicists' excitement was proportional to how long they'd waited. Then read why the Higgs matters: without its field, electrons and quarks would be massless and atoms could never form.

name: Graphene (2004)
teaser: Graphene — a single layer of carbon atoms in a honeycomb lattice, one atom thick — was isolated in 2004 by Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov using sticky tape to peel layers off graphite. It's 200 times stronger than steel, flexible, nearly transparent, and conducts electricity better than copper; the pair won the 2010 Nobel.

exploreAction.targetName: The 2004 Science paper + the scotch-tape method video
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the 'scotch tape method' video — the Nobel-winning discovery used ordinary adhesive tape — and read the 2004 Science paper's famously modest title ('Electric Field Effect in Atomically Thin Carbon Films'). Then read why it's a wonder material: its electrons move as if massless, which is what makes its conductivity so remarkable.

name: The First Black Hole Image (2019)
teaser: The first image of a black hole — M87*, the supermassive black hole at the center of galaxy M87, 55 million light-years away — was released on 10 April 2019. It required the Event Horizon Telescope, an array of eight radio observatories spread across the planet acting as one Earth-sized telescope, and it showed the predicted ring of light around darkness.

exploreAction.targetName: The 2019 M87* image + the EHT data-combining process
exploreAction.instruction: Single out the image's structure: the bright orange ring is not the black hole itself but the glowing gas falling into it, lensed by gravity into a circle — the 'photon ring.' Then read how the image was made: each observatory recorded petabytes of data, which was physically shipped on hard drives (the internet was too slow) and combined in a computer to synthesize an Earth-sized aperture.

name: Chaos Theory (1960s)
teaser: Chaos theory was born in 1961 when meteorologist Edward Lorenz rounded a weather-simulation number from 0.506127 to 0.506 and got a completely different forecast — the discovery that tiny changes in initial conditions produce vastly different outcomes. His 1963 paper, 'Deterministic Nonperiodic Flow,' founded the field.

exploreAction.targetName: Lorenz's 1963 'Deterministic Nonperiodic Flow' + the attractor plots
exploreAction.instruction: Read Lorenz's own account of the rounding-error moment, then look at his famous 'Lorenz attractor' plots — the butterfly-shaped diagram that shows chaotic systems have hidden order: the paths never repeat, but they always stay on the same strange attractor. That paradox — deterministic but unpredictable — is the field's core, and it's why weather can be forecast days, not months, ahead.

name: The World Wide Web (1989)
teaser: Tim Berners-Lee proposed the World Wide Web in March 1989 at CERN — a way to link documents over the internet — and his boss wrote on the cover sheet the most famous memo in computing: 'Vague but exciting.' He built the first browser, server, and webpage (info.cern.ch) by 1991, and gave the technology away rather than patent it.

exploreAction.targetName: Berners-Lee's 1989 proposal + the preserved first website
exploreAction.instruction: Read the 1989 proposal ('Information Management: A Proposal') and notice what Berners-Lee got right: the Web was designed for collaboration, with no central control. Then visit the first website's preserved page and read his summary of the project — the Web was conceived as a system for scientists sharing data, and its inventors never imagined shopping, social media, or search engines.

name: Public Key Cryptography (1976)
teaser: Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman published public-key cryptography in 1976 — the idea that two strangers can agree on a secret key over an open channel, enabling secure communication without a shared secret. Three years later, Rivest, Shamir, and Adleman built RSA on their foundation, the encryption behind most of the modern internet.

exploreAction.targetName: Diffie–Hellman 1976 'New Directions in Cryptography' + the GCHQ priority dispute
exploreAction.instruction: Read the 1976 paper's framing — the 'two-channel cryptography' problem — and understand the core idea: a mathematical function that is easy to compute one way and hard to invert, letting you publish the 'lock' and keep the 'key.' Then read the British twist: GCHQ's James Ellis and Clifford Cocks had invented the same idea years earlier, in secret, which was only declassified in 1997.

name: Deep Learning Neural Networks (2012)
teaser: Modern deep learning arrived in 2012 when Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, and Geoffrey Hinton entered AlexNet — a deep neural network trained on GPUs — in the ImageNet competition and halved the error rate of every previous system overnight. The technique had existed since the 1980s; the breakthrough was scale and compute.

exploreAction.targetName: The 2012 AlexNet ImageNet paper + the error-rate comparison
exploreAction.instruction: Read the AlexNet paper and notice what actually changed: the network had 60 million parameters trained on 1.2 million images over days of GPU time, and its error rate (15.3%) crushed the runner-up's 26.2%. The lesson the field took from it — that bigger networks, more data, and more compute beat cleverer algorithms — set the agenda for the next decade of AI.

name: Self-Driving Cars (2010s)
teaser: The modern self-driving era began in 2004 with the DARPA Grand Challenge — a 142-mile desert race in which every vehicle failed, with the best covering only 7 miles. A year later, Stanford's Stanley finished the course, and by 2009 Google had launched its self-driving project (now Waymo) that would log millions of miles of public-road testing.

exploreAction.targetName: The 2004 DARPA Grand Challenge + Stanley's 2005 win
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the 2004 DARPA race footage — the robots crashing, catching fire, and wandering into the desert — and notice what the failure taught the field: the hard problem is not driving but perception under uncertainty. Then read about the 2005 Stanford win and the lidar-based approach Google adopted: the modern stack (lidar + maps + learning) descends directly from those early races.

name: The Structure of the Ribosome (2000)
teaser: The ribosome — the molecular machine that builds proteins — was mapped at atomic resolution in 2000 by three teams led by Venki Ramakrishnan, Thomas Steitz, and Ada Yonath, who shared the 2009 Nobel. Yonath had spent 20 years crystallizing ribosomes, a project colleagues called impossible; the ribosome is the largest structure ever solved with X-ray crystallography at the time.

exploreAction.targetName: The 2000 ribosome structures — the Nobel-winning crystallography
exploreAction.instruction: Focus on a ribbon diagram of the ribosome and notice its two halves — the small subunit that reads the genetic code and the large subunit that stitches amino acids together. Then read about Yonath's perseverance: she crystallized ribosomes from heat-loving bacteria that survive in hot springs, because their ribosomes are robust enough to form crystals.

name: Apoptosis (1972)
teaser: Apoptosis — programmed cell death — was named in 1972 by John Kerr, Andrew Wyllie, and Alastair Currie, who realized that cells have a built-in suicide program: your body kills about 50 billion cells every day as a routine part of life. The word is Greek for 'falling off,' as leaves from a tree, and cancer is partly a failure of this program.

exploreAction.targetName: The 1972 Kerr–Wyllie–Currie paper + the C. elegans cell-lineage work
exploreAction.instruction: Read the 1972 paper where the word was coined — Kerr had first described the cell-death pattern in 1965 while studying liver cells — and notice the authors' insight: this death was not injury but choreography. Then read about the C. elegans work (Horvitz, Sulston, Brenner, Nobel 2002) that found the genes running the program: the worm's fixed cell lineage made the suicide genes visible.

name: The First Clone (Dolly 1996)
teaser: Dolly the sheep, born 5 July 1996 at the Roslin Institute, was the first mammal cloned from an adult cell — created by transferring the nucleus of a mammary-gland cell into an egg. Named after Dolly Parton (because the donor cell came from a mammary gland), she was announced in 1997 and immediately became the most famous animal in science.

exploreAction.targetName: Wilmut's 1997 Nature paper on Dolly + her health timeline
exploreAction.instruction: Read the 1997 Nature paper and notice what the media missed: the cloning had a success rate of about 1 in 277 attempts, and Dolly was the only lamb born from 29 embryos that survived. Then read the follow-up: Dolly developed arthritis and lung disease and was euthanized in 2003, and her early death fueled the debate about whether clones age prematurely — a question still not fully settled.

name: The Microbiome (2010s)
teaser: The human microbiome — the community of ~100 trillion bacteria, fungi, and viruses living in and on your body — was mapped at scale by the Human Microbiome Project, launched in 2007. The bacteria in your gut weigh about as much as your brain, outnumber your own cells (though the ratio is closer to 1:1 than the old 10:1 claim), and are implicated in everything from digestion to mood.

exploreAction.targetName: The Human Microbiome Project results + the gut-brain evidence review
exploreAction.instruction: Read the Human Microbiome Project's results and notice the surprise: each person's microbiome is as individual as a fingerprint, and the same 'species' differ between people at the strain level. Then read the gut-brain research carefully — the 'gut feeling' studies are real but the marketing has outpaced the science: most microbiome claims in wellness products are not yet supported by trials.

name: The Ozone Layer Recovery (ongoing)
teaser: The ozone hole over Antarctica — discovered in 1985 by a British team led by Joe Farman, who was initially afraid his instruments were broken — was caused by CFCs, chemicals in spray cans and refrigerants. The 1987 Montreal Protocol banned them, the only UN treaty ratified by every country on Earth, and the hole is now slowly healing, expected to close around 2066.

exploreAction.targetName: Farman's 1985 Nature paper + the Montreal Protocol timeline
exploreAction.instruction: Read Farman's 1985 Nature paper and notice what made it convincing: the British team's ground measurements showed a 40% ozone loss that matched nothing in the models, and the American satellite data had been discarding the same readings as 'errors.' Then read the Montreal Protocol story: the treaty worked because industry had alternatives ready, and the ozone layer's recovery is the existence proof that global environmental action can succeed.

name: The Keeling Curve (1958)
teaser: The Keeling Curve — the longest continuous record of atmospheric CO2 — began in 1958 when Charles David Keeling set up instruments at Mauna Loa, Hawaii, high enough to sample well-mixed air. The curve's sawtooth pattern (plants breathing CO2 in summer, releasing it in winter) rides a steady rise from 315 ppm in 1958 to over 420 ppm today — a 34% increase.

exploreAction.targetName: The full Keeling Curve — the sawtooth and the rising baseline
exploreAction.instruction: Start with the full curve and separate the two signals: the annual sawtooth is the Earth's breathing, and the rising baseline is fossil-fuel emissions accumulating in the atmosphere. Then read why Keeling chose Mauna Loa: at 3,400 meters in the Pacific, the air is well-mixed and far from local sources, making the record a measure of the whole planet, not one country.

name: The Extinction of the Dinosaurs (1980)
teaser: In 1980, physicist Luis Alvarez and his geologist son Walter proposed that the dinosaurs were killed by an asteroid: a thin layer of iridium — an element rare on Earth but common in asteroids — at the 66-million-year-old K-Pg boundary in rocks worldwide. The theory was mocked for a decade until the Chicxulub crater, 180 km wide, was found in the Gulf of Mexico in 1991.

exploreAction.targetName: The 1980 Alvarez paper + the Chicxulub crater discovery
exploreAction.instruction: Read the 1980 Science paper and notice the evidence chain: iridium at 30 times background levels, found in the exact layer where the dinosaurs vanish, at sites across the globe. Then read the Chicxulub discovery — the crater's age matches the boundary to within 30,000 years, and its size implies an impactor roughly 10 km across. The paper that was dismissed as 'unfalsifiable' is now the standard account.

name: Homo Naledi (2013)
teaser: In 2013, cavers squeezed through a 12-centimeter gap into the Rising Star cave in South Africa and found over 1,550 fossil fragments of a new human relative, Homo naledi — a small-brained hominin with hands built for climbing, announced in 2015 by Lee Berger's team. The find raised a radical claim: that naledi may have deliberately buried its dead, a behavior previously thought unique to modern humans.

exploreAction.targetName: The 2015 Homo naledi announcements + the burial debate
exploreAction.instruction: Read the 2015 eLife papers and notice what makes naledi strange: a brain one-third the size of ours combined with human-like hands and feet, dated to only ~250,000 years ago — potentially coexisting with early Homo sapiens. Then read the contested burial claim (2023): the team argues the remains' arrangement and the cave's depth imply intentional deposition, and the debate over that interpretation is ongoing and fierce.

name: Fire (prehistoric)
teaser: Controlled fire is one of humanity's oldest technologies, with the earliest strong evidence — ash, burned bone, and heat-altered tools — at Wonderwerk Cave in South Africa dating to about one million years ago. Cooking was the revolution within the revolution: cooked food is easier to digest, and the 'expensive tissue hypothesis' argues the extra energy allowed our ancestors' brains to grow.

exploreAction.targetName: The Wonderwerk Cave hearth evidence + the cooking hypothesis
exploreAction.instruction: Read the Wonderwerk Cave evidence — the oldest well-accepted hearth, a million years old, in a cave in the Kalahari — and compare it with the alternative claims: some sites in Kenya suggest fire use 1.5 million years ago, but the evidence is contested. Then read the cooking argument: Richard Wrangham's claim that cooked food, not tools or language, is the key innovation that made us human is controversial but illuminating.

name: Agriculture (10000 BC)
teaser: Agriculture — the domestication of plants and animals — began independently in at least seven regions, with wheat and barley in the Fertile Crescent around 10,000–12,000 years ago, rice in China, maize in Mesoamerica, and potatoes in the Andes. The shift from hunting to farming is called the Neolithic Revolution, and it was not obviously an improvement: early farmers were shorter and sicker than the hunter-gatherers they replaced.

exploreAction.targetName: The Göbekli Tepe chronology vs. the standard Neolithic story
exploreAction.instruction: Read the 'Göbekli Tepe problem': the monumental stone temple in Turkey, built ~9600 BC by pre-agricultural people, suggests the ritual impulse came first and farming followed to feed the gatherings — inverting the standard story that farming created civilization. Then weigh the evidence: skeletons show early farmers had more cavities, anemia, and infectious disease than foragers, yet farming won because it fed far more people per acre.

name: The Printing Press (1440)
teaser: Gutenberg's printing press (c. 1440) combined movable metal type with a wine press, and by 1500 — within 50 years — an estimated 20 million books had been printed across Europe, versus the thousands of manuscripts scribes had produced in the previous century. The first product was the 42-line Bible, and the technology is often credited with making the Reformation possible.

exploreAction.targetName: The Gutenberg 42-line Bible + the spread of printing 1450–1500
exploreAction.instruction: Peer at a Gutenberg Bible page and notice what printing changed: identical text in identical type, produced in weeks instead of a year per copy. Then read the numbers of the press's spread — printing shops appeared in 255 cities within 50 years, and the price of books collapsed — and consider the argument that the press's real product was not books but standardization: identical texts made shared arguments possible at continental scale.

name: Electricity (1800)
teaser: The modern age of electricity began in 1800 when Alessandro Volta built the first battery — the voltaic pile, stacks of zinc and copper discs separated by brine-soaked paper — producing a steady, reliable current for the first time. The discovery grew out of a feud: Volta built it to disprove Galvani's claim that animal tissue generated 'animal electricity.'.

exploreAction.targetName: Volta's 1800 letter describing the pile + the electrolysis experiments
exploreAction.instruction: Read the story of the Galvani–Volta feud: Galvani saw frog legs twitch when touched with two metals and concluded the electricity came from the animal; Volta proved it came from the two metals and made the frog irrelevant. Then find the earliest consequence: within months of the pile's announcement, scientists used its current to split water into hydrogen and oxygen — electrolysis, the parent of electrochemistry.

name: The Light Bulb (1879)
teaser: Thomas Edison's incandescent bulb of 1879 was not the first electric light — but it was the first practical one: a carbon filament in a vacuum that lasted over 1,200 hours. The real invention was the system around it: Edison designed the bulb, the generator, the wiring, and the meter as one package, which is why he, not his predecessors, is remembered.

exploreAction.targetName: Edison's 1879 filament work vs. Swan's earlier lamp
exploreAction.instruction: Read the '1,200 experiments' account — Edison's own tally of filament materials tested — and notice what the story omits: Joseph Swan had demonstrated a working carbon-filament lamp in Britain a year earlier, and the two settled patent disputes by merging. Then read what made Edison's version win: not the bulb itself but the integrated electrical grid he built to sell it.

name: Television (1927)
teaser: Philo Farnsworth transmitted the first all-electronic television image on 7 September 1927 — a single straight line, which he celebrated by drawing a dollar sign to show his wife the machine could pay. He was 21, working in a Los Angeles lab funded by investors, and he beat the mechanical scanning systems of John Logie Baird by using an electron beam instead of spinning discs.

exploreAction.targetName: Farnsworth's 1927 image dissector + the RCA patent fight
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the 1927 reconstruction or read Farnsworth's patent description and notice the key move: the 'image dissector' scanned the picture with an electron beam, line by line, with no moving parts — the principle behind every TV since.

name: The Microprocessor (1971)
teaser: Intel's 4004, released in November 1971, was the first microprocessor — an entire computer's CPU on a single chip, with 2,300 transistors, built for a Japanese calculator company that had outgrown its custom chips. The team of three (Federico Faggin, Marcian Hoff, Stan Mazor) created the architecture that every modern computer still descends from.

exploreAction.targetName: The Intel 4004's 1971 debut + the Busicom rights buyback
exploreAction.instruction: Read the 4004's spec sheet and notice the scale: 2,300 transistors on a chip smaller than a fingernail, running at 740 kHz — slower than a modern calculator — but it replaced a room of electronics. Then read the business accident: Intel had designed the chip for Busicom, then bought back the rights when the calculator company hit financial trouble, which is why the 'microprocessor' became Intel's product rather than one customer's component.

name: The Search Engine (1996)
teaser: Google began in 1996 as 'BackRub,' a Stanford research project by Larry Page and Sergey Brin that ranked web pages by counting links — the insight that a link is a vote. The system, PageRank, was good enough that the pair dropped out of their PhDs to found a company in 1998, and 'googling' entered the language within a few years.

exploreAction.targetName: The 1998 'Anatomy of a Search Engine' paper + the BackRub origin
exploreAction.instruction: Read the 1998 Stanford paper ('The Anatomy of a Large-Scale Hypertextual Web Search Engine') and notice what was radical: instead of counting keyword matches, PageRank treated the web's link structure as a popularity signal, and it worked on pages the crawler had never seen ranked. Then read how the founders tried to sell the technology — Excite and Yahoo both passed — before raising venture money and running the company from a garage.

name: The Structure of DNA (1953)
teaser: Watson and Crick published the double helix on 25 April 1953 in a 900-word Nature paper — the most famous understatement in science: 'It has not escaped our notice that the specific pairing we have postulated immediately suggests a possible copying mechanism for the genetic material.' The structure explained heredity at a stroke, and the paper ended by thanking no one for the data it used.

exploreAction.targetName: The 25 April 1953 Nature paper — the double-helix announcement
exploreAction.instruction: Read the 1953 Nature paper in full — it's short enough to read twice — and notice what it does and doesn't say: the structure is stated as a fact with minimal evidence, and the crucial X-ray image (Photo 51, taken by Rosalind Franklin) is acknowledged only in a final footnote.

name: Anesthesia (1846)
teaser: On 16 October 1846, dentist William Morton administered ether to a patient while surgeon John Collins Warren removed a tumor from his neck — and the patient reported no pain. Witness Oliver Wendell Holmes called the moment 'the annihilation of pain,' and the news circled the world within months: surgery without anesthesia had been limited to amputations measured in minutes.

exploreAction.targetName: The 16 October 1846 Ether Day demonstration
exploreAction.instruction: Read the first-person account of 'Ether Day' and notice the stakes: the patient, Gilbert Abbott, was undergoing a procedure that would previously have meant being held down.

name: Pasteurization (1864)
teaser: Louis Pasteur's pasteurization of 1864 — heating wine and beer to 50–60°C to kill the microbes that spoiled them — was a practical fix for a commercial crisis, and it became the proof of his germ theory. The French wine industry was losing exports to spoilage; Pasteur's process saved it, and the same idea now protects milk worldwide.

exploreAction.targetName: Pasteur's 1864 wine-spoilage experiments
exploreAction.instruction: Read Pasteur's own account of the experiments and notice the industrial framing: he was solving a business problem (soured wine), not a public-health one, and his heating process was calibrated to kill the spoilage microbes while preserving flavor. Then connect it to the bigger fight: pasteurization was Pasteur's applied proof of the germ theory he was then fighting to establish against the 'spontaneous generation' view.

name: X-Rays (1895)
teaser: Wilhelm Röntgen discovered X-rays on 8 November 1895 while testing whether cathode rays could pass through cardboard — a screen across the room glowed, and the radiation that caused it passed through everything but bone. He took the first X-ray photo, of his wife's hand, and won the first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901; doctors were using X-rays within months.

exploreAction.targetName: Röntgen's first X-ray image of his wife's hand
exploreAction.instruction: Look at Röntgen's first image — his wife Bertha's hand, the bones and wedding ring visible — and read her reported reaction ('I have seen my death'). Then read the discovery's method: Röntgen worked alone for six weeks in his lab, refused to patent the discovery, and gave his notes and apparatus to the scientific community, which is why X-ray use spread so fast.

name: The Electron (1897)
teaser: J.J. Thomson identified the electron in 1897 by measuring how cathode rays bent in magnetic and electric fields — showing they were particles, and that those particles were lighter than any atom: about 1/1836 the mass of a hydrogen atom. It was the first subatomic particle ever found, and it overturned the idea that atoms were indivisible.

exploreAction.targetName: Thomson's 1897 'Cathode Rays' paper — the mass-to-charge measurement
exploreAction.instruction: Read the 1897 paper ('Cathode Rays') and follow the measurement: Thomson deflected the rays with electric and magnetic fields, and the balance of the two deflections let him compute the particle's mass-to-charge ratio — far smaller than an ion's. Then read the significance: if the electron came from inside atoms, atoms had structure, and the hunt for that structure (Rutherford's nucleus, 1911) followed directly.

name: Relativity (1905)
teaser: Einstein's special relativity, published in 1905 — his 'miracle year,' when he also explained the photoelectric effect, Brownian motion, and mass-energy equivalence — showed that space and time are not absolute: moving clocks run slow, moving rulers shrink, and nothing can exceed the speed of light. The equation E=mc², its most famous consequence, was in the same year's papers.

exploreAction.targetName: Einstein's 1905 'Zur Elektrodynamik bewegter Körper' — the two postulates
exploreAction.instruction: Read the 1905 paper's two postulates — the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames, and light's speed is constant regardless of the observer's motion — and then work through the consequence Einstein draws: if both hold, simultaneity must be relative, and time itself stretches.

name: The Proton (1919)
teaser: Ernest Rutherford identified the proton in 1919 by firing alpha particles at nitrogen and knocking hydrogen nuclei out of the atoms — the first artificial transmutation of one element into another, 5,000 years after the alchemists gave up. He named the hydrogen nucleus 'proton' in 1920, from the Greek for 'first.'.

exploreAction.targetName: Rutherford's 1919 transmutation experiments
exploreAction.instruction: Read the 1919 paper's experiment and notice the elegance: alpha particles (helium nuclei) striking nitrogen produced oxygen and a hydrogen nucleus, which Rutherford recognized as the building block inside every atom. Then read the naming story — Rutherford proposed 'proton' from the Greek 'protos' (first) — and connect it to the model of the atom he was assembling: positive nucleus, electrons outside, the whole thing mostly empty space.

name: Nuclear Fission (1938)
teaser: Nuclear fission was discovered in December 1938 when Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann bombarded uranium with neutrons and found barium — an atom half uranium's size — a result they could not explain. The explanation came from Lise Meitner, in exile in Sweden, who with her nephew Otto Frisch named the process 'fission' in a letter, and calculated the enormous energy released.

exploreAction.targetName: The 1938 barium experiment + the Meitner–Frisch explanation
exploreAction.instruction: Read the sequence of the discovery and notice who was where: Meitner, Jewish, had fled Berlin months earlier; Hahn wrote to her in Stockholm with the baffling barium result, and she worked out the physics — the uranium nucleus had split, and the mass difference had become energy via E=mc².

name: The Laser (1960)
teaser: Theodore Maiman built the first working laser on 16 May 1960 at Hughes Research Laboratories — a ruby rod flashed with a photographer's lamp, producing the first beam of coherent light. The press called it 'a solution looking for a problem'; sixty years later, lasers read your discs, cut your metal, measure the Moon, and run fiber-optic internet.

exploreAction.targetName: Maiman's 1960 ruby laser + its first applications timeline
exploreAction.instruction: Read Maiman's own account of the breakthrough and notice how it was dismissed: his Nature paper was initially rejected (the editors thought it too sensational), and the field's leaders believed a ruby laser couldn't work because the numbers said the ruby would need too much pumping.

name: Pulsars (1967)
teaser: Pulsars were discovered in 1967 by Jocelyn Bell Burnell, a 24-year-old graduate student who noticed 'scruff' — a regular pulse of radio waves, 1.3 seconds apart, in her chart recordings. She and her supervisor Anthony Hewish briefly nicknamed the source LGM-1 ('Little Green Men') before identifying it as a rotating neutron star — the collapsed corpse of a massive star, spinning and beaming like a lighthouse.

exploreAction.targetName: Bell Burnell's 1967 'scruff' discovery + the 1974 Nobel exclusion
exploreAction.instruction: Read Bell Burnell's account of the discovery and notice the conditions: she was analyzing 120 feet of chart paper per day by eye, and the signal's extreme regularity — so precise it initially looked artificial — is what made her rule out interference.

name: The Ozone Hole (1985)
teaser: The ozone hole was discovered in 1985 by a small British Antarctic Survey team led by Joe Farman — who initially thought his instruments were broken when they showed a 40% seasonal loss of ozone over Halley Bay. NASA's satellite had seen the same depletion for years but its software had been programmed to discard the readings as impossible errors.

exploreAction.targetName: Farman's 1985 Nature paper + the NASA data-discarding story
exploreAction.instruction: Read Farman's 1985 Nature paper and the dramatic footnote it contains: the measurements had actually begun in the 1970s, and the ozone loss appeared suddenly in the late 1970s — a breakpoint that pointed straight at CFCs.

name: The Higgs Boson (2012)
teaser: The Higgs boson — the last missing piece of the Standard Model — was discovered on 4 July 2012 at CERN's Large Hadron Collider, ending a search that had run since the particle was predicted in 1964. The LHC had been running for barely two years; the discovery required 3,000 physicists and collisions at 13 trillion electron-volts.

exploreAction.targetName: The 4 July 2012 Higgs seminar + the 5-sigma standard
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the 4 July 2012 seminar (the one where Peter Higgs, now 83, wiped his glasses and wept) and read the announcement's language: the teams reported a 'new boson' at 125 GeV with 5-sigma confidence — the threshold particle physicists use for 'discovery' instead of 'evidence.' Then read what a 5-sigma standard means: it's the probability of a false alarm at about 1 in 3.5 million, a bar set after a series of famous near-misses in the field.

name: The Big Bang Theory
teaser: The Big Bang theory — that the universe began as an extremely hot, dense point and has been expanding ever since — was first proposed by Belgian priest and physicist Georges Lemaître in 1927 and confirmed by Hubble's 1929 discovery that galaxies are rushing apart. The name was coined dismissively by Fred Hoyle in 1949, and the theory's decisive evidence came in 1964 with the accidental discovery of the cosmic microwave background.

exploreAction.targetName: The 1964 cosmic microwave background discovery + the Hubble expansion
exploreAction.instruction: Read the evidence chain in order: Lemaître's 1927 paper (published two years before Hubble's), Hubble's redshift measurements, and then the 1964 discovery by Penzias and Wilson — two radio astronomers who spent a year trying to remove an annoying 'noise' from their antenna before realizing it was the afterglow of the Big Bang itself.

name: Mendelian Genetics (1866)
teaser: Gregor Mendel's pea experiments — 22,000 plants, seven traits, eight years in a monastery garden — established the laws of heredity in 1866, and were then ignored for 35 years until three botanists independently rediscovered them in 1900. Mendel died in 1884 without knowing his work would found the science of genetics; the word 'genetics' wasn't even coined until 1905.

exploreAction.targetName: Mendel's 1866 pea experiments + the 1900 rediscovery
exploreAction.instruction: Read Mendel's 1866 paper and notice the mathematics that made it radical: he counted, rather than described, tracking each trait across generations and finding the 3:1 ratio that implied discrete hereditary 'factors' (which we now call genes).

name: The Electron Microscope (1931)
teaser: Ernst Ruska built the first electron microscope in 1931, using a beam of electrons — whose wavelength is about 100,000 times shorter than light's — to image objects far below the resolution of any optical microscope. It took the 1986 Nobel Prize, and modern electron microscopes resolve individual atoms; the instrument revealed the viruses and cell structures that light could never show.

exploreAction.targetName: Ruska's 1931 electron microscope + the wavelength-resolution comparison
exploreAction.instruction: Read the physics of the resolution limit first: an optical microscope cannot resolve objects smaller than about half the wavelength of light (~200 nanometers), which is why viruses were invisible until the electron microscope. Then read Ruska's insight: electrons are particles with a wavelength, and a magnetic 'lens' can focus them the way glass focuses light.

name: The First Antibiotic (1932)
teaser: The first antibacterial drug that could be mass-produced was Prontosil, developed by Gerhard Domagk in 1932 and used from 1935 — a red dye that cured bacterial infections in mice and, famously, Domagk's own daughter. Penicillin had been discovered in 1928 but couldn't be mass-produced until the 1940s; the sulfa drugs were the first to save lives at scale, and Domagk won the 1939 Nobel.

exploreAction.targetName: Domagk's 1932 Prontosil + the penicillin timeline
exploreAction.instruction: Read the Prontosil story and its twist: the dye itself was inactive — it worked because the body metabolized it into the active sulfanilamide, which is why the later, colorless sulfa drugs worked identically.

name: The Structure of Insulin (1969)
teaser: Dorothy Hodgkin solved the three-dimensional structure of insulin in 1969 — the climax of 35 years of work — having already deciphered penicillin and vitamin B12, for which she won the 1964 Nobel. By the end she was tracing electron-density maps with a magnifying glass, her hands crippled by rheumatoid arthritis; the structure she produced is the one still taught.

exploreAction.targetName: Hodgkin's 1969 insulin structure + the synthetic insulin outcome
exploreAction.instruction: Read about the 35-year span and notice what changed along the way: Hodgkin had been working on insulin since 1934, but the structure required better X-ray sources and computers, so her success was timed to the technology's maturity as much as her patience.

name: MRI Imaging (1973)
teaser: MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) was born in 1973 when Paul Lauterbur published the first cross-sectional NMR image, made by adding magnetic field gradients to nuclear magnetic resonance.

exploreAction.targetName: Lauterbur's 1973 Nature paper + the Nobel controversy
exploreAction.instruction: Read Lauterbur's 1973 Nature paper — titled 'Image Formation by Induced Local Interactions: Examples Employing Nuclear Magnetic Resonance' — and notice the modesty of the first image: a pair of water-filled tubes.

name: The Human Genome Project (2003)
teaser: The Human Genome Project — 13 years, 20 labs, $3 billion, and 3 billion base pairs — produced a complete draft of the human genetic code in 2000 and the finished sequence in 2003. The genome turned out to contain roughly 20,000 protein-coding genes — fewer than a grape — and the project's real legacy is the technology it forced into existence.

exploreAction.targetName: The 2001 draft sequence announcement + the gene-count surprise
exploreAction.instruction: Read the 2001 announcement history and notice the race: a private company, Celera, ran a parallel genome project, and the public project published simultaneously to avoid losing the credit.

name: RNA Interference (1998)
teaser: RNA interference — the discovery that double-stranded RNA silences genes — was announced by Andrew Fire and Craig Mello in a 1998 Nature paper, and it won the 2006 Nobel. The mechanism turned out to be an ancient immune system: cells use small RNAs to find and destroy foreign or duplicate genetic messages, and scientists can hijack it to switch off any gene on demand.

exploreAction.targetName: Fire & Mello's 1998 Nature paper on RNAi
exploreAction.instruction: Read the 1998 Nature paper and notice the unglamorous details: Fire and Mello injected double-stranded RNA into C. elegans worms and watched specific genes go silent — and the double-stranded form worked a hundredfold better than single strands, which is the clue that cracked the mechanism.

name: mRNA Vaccines (2020)
teaser: The mRNA vaccines that ended the COVID-19 pandemic's worst phase were the product of a 40-year scientific arc: messenger RNA — the molecule cells use to read genes — repurposed as a drug-delivery system. The key work was done in 2005 by Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman, who solved the problem of mRNA triggering inflammation; they shared the 2023 Nobel.

exploreAction.targetName: The 2005 Karikó–Weissman paper + the 2020 vaccine deployment
exploreAction.instruction: Read the 2005 Karikó–Weissman paper and notice the drama the award ceremony glossed over: Karikó had been demoted at her university and was a decade into grant rejections when she and Weissman showed that modified nucleosides let mRNA slip past the immune system. Then read the 2020 application: the vaccine instructs cells to make the spike protein, and the 'm' in mRNA is the whole revolution — the message can be rewritten for any virus in weeks.

name: Dark Energy (1998)
teaser: Dark energy — the unknown force accelerating the universe's expansion — was inferred in 1998 from distant supernovae that were dimmer than they should be, meaning the expansion isn't slowing as gravity demands but speeding up. It accounts for about 68% of the universe's total content, yet nobody knows what it is; the 2011 Nobel went to the two teams' leaders.

exploreAction.targetName: The 1998 accelerating-expansion papers + the vacuum-energy problem
exploreAction.instruction: Read the 1998 papers and notice what the discoverers expected to find: both teams designed the experiment to measure deceleration — the universe slowing under gravity — and both were forced by their own data to conclude the opposite.

name: Neutrino Oscillations (1998)
teaser: In 1998, the Super-Kamiokande detector in Japan announced that neutrinos — the universe's most ghostly particles, which pass through the Earth by the trillions — change flavor as they travel, a phenomenon called oscillation. The discovery proved neutrinos have mass, contradicting the Standard Model's assumption and forcing a rewrite of physics; it brought the 2015 Nobel to Takaaki Kajita (and, for solar neutrinos, Arthur McDonald).

exploreAction.targetName: The 1998 Super-Kamiokande announcement + the oscillation method
exploreAction.instruction: Read how the measurement works: Super-Kamiokande is a 50,000-ton tank of pure water lined with 13,000 light detectors, built to catch the rare flashes when a neutrino collides with a water molecule. The oscillation signature showed up as a deficit: neutrinos created in the atmosphere as muon-type were arriving as fewer muon-neutrinos than expected, with the deficit growing with distance — the telltale of flavor-switching in flight.

name: Topological Insulators (2007)
teaser: Topological insulators — materials that insulate electricity in their interior while conducting it perfectly along their surfaces — were predicted and observed in the late 2000s, and they showed that the shape of an electron's wavefunction ('topology') can dictate a material's properties as surely as its chemistry. The field's pioneers won the 2016 Nobel, and the materials are candidates for fault-tolerant quantum computers.

exploreAction.targetName: The 2007 topological insulator experiments + the Möbius analogy
exploreAction.instruction: Read the concept through the familiar example the papers use: a Möbius strip's twist is a global property you can't remove by local changes — similarly, the 'twist' in an electron's quantum state can't be undone by impurities, which is why the surface conduction is so robust.

name: Fullerenes (1985)
teaser: Buckminsterfullerene — a molecule of 60 carbon atoms arranged like a soccer ball — was discovered in 1985 by Harold Kroto, Richard Smalley, and Robert Curl, who vaporized graphite with a laser and found the carbon atoms assembling themselves into the ball. They named it after Buckminster Fuller, inventor of the geodesic dome, and won the 1996 Nobel; the discovery opened the field of carbon nanostructures that led to nanotubes and graphene.

exploreAction.targetName: The 1985 laser-vaporization experiment + the C60 structure insight
exploreAction.instruction: Read the discovery story and notice the accident within the discovery: the team was trying to understand carbon chains in space (Kroto's interest) and found instead a 60-atom molecule so stable it shouldn't have formed by chance. The 'aha' came when Smalley realized the soccer-ball structure would be perfectly stable.

name: The Theory of Everything (ongoing)
teaser: A 'theory of everything' — one set of equations uniting gravity with quantum mechanics — has been the holy grail of physics for a century, since Einstein spent his last 30 years chasing it and failed. String theory and loop quantum gravity are the leading candidates, but neither has produced a single experimentally confirmed prediction, and the quest is, famously, unfinished.

exploreAction.targetName: The gravity-vs-quantum contradiction + the two leading candidates
exploreAction.instruction: Read why gravity refuses to fit: quantum mechanics describes the very small with probabilistic waves, general relativity describes the very large with smooth spacetime, and the two formalisms contradict each other at the extremes — inside black holes and at the universe's first instant. Then read the candidates honestly: string theory predicts extra dimensions and has no confirmed experiment; loop quantum gravity is more modest but also untested.

name: Fractals (1975)
teaser: Benoit Mandelbrot coined the word 'fractal' in 1975 for shapes whose complexity repeats at every scale — a coastline measured with a longer ruler gets longer without limit. His 1967 paper, 'How Long Is the Coast of Britain?,' founded the field, and the Mandelbrot set he visualized in 1980 became the most famous mathematical image ever made, its boundary infinitely detailed by a two-line formula.

exploreAction.targetName: Mandelbrot's 'How Long Is the Coast of Britain?' + the Mandelbrot set
exploreAction.instruction: Read the 1967 coastline paper and follow the paradox: if you measure a coastline with 100 km rulers you get one answer; with 10 km rulers you get a longer one, and the length grows without bound as the rulers shrink — the coast is a fractal, with a dimension between 1 and 2.

name: The Internet Protocol (1974)
teaser: TCP/IP — the protocol pair that lets every computer on Earth talk to every other — was designed by Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn in 1974, in a paper titled 'A Protocol for Packet Network Intercommunication.' The internet's birth is usually dated to 1 January 1983, when the ARPANET switched over to the new protocol in a single coordinated 'flag day.'.

exploreAction.targetName: The 1974 Cerf–Kahn paper + the 1983 flag day
exploreAction.instruction: Read the 1974 paper and notice the design principle that made it universal: the protocol doesn't care what kind of network carries the packets, so radio, satellite, and wired networks could all interoperate — that's the 'inter' in 'internet.' Then read the 1983 flag-day story: the ARPANET cut over to TCP/IP overnight, with zero tolerance for error, and the network that had connected a few universities became the skeleton of a worldwide system.

name: The Smartphone (2007)
teaser: The smartphone era is usually dated to 9 January 2007, when Steve Jobs introduced the iPhone — a phone, an iPod, and an internet communicator in one touchscreen device with no keyboard. Smartphones themselves predate it (IBM's Simon, 1992), but the iPhone's app store and capacitive touchscreen defined the form every phone since has copied, and there are now more smartphones on Earth than people with bank accounts.

exploreAction.targetName: The 9 January 2007 iPhone keynote + the App Store's arrival
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the 2007 keynote and notice what Jobs emphasized — 'a revolutionary user interface' — and what he didn't mention: there were no apps initially; the App Store arrived a year later and created the ecosystem that made the device a platform. Then read the numbers: by 2016, two billion people had smartphones, and the devices had become the primary camera, map, and bank for most of humanity — a scale no previous technology reached in a decade.

name: AlphaFold Protein Folding (2020)
teaser: AlphaFold — DeepMind's neural network — cracked protein structure prediction in 2020, solving a problem biologists had chased for 50 years: given a protein's amino-acid sequence, predict the 3D shape it folds into. In the biennial CASP competition it scored near-experimental accuracy, and in 2024 its developers shared the Nobel in Chemistry with protein-design pioneer David Baker.

exploreAction.targetName: The 2020 CASP14 results + the 2022 proteome-wide expansion
exploreAction.instruction: Read why folding matters: a protein's shape determines what it does, and knowing a protein's structure is the foundation of drug design — but experimental methods (X-ray crystallography, cryo-EM) can take months or years per protein.

name: Reusable Rockets (2015)
teaser: On 21 December 2015, SpaceX landed a Falcon 9 rocket booster upright on a landing pad — the first time an orbital-class rocket had flown again after delivering its payload. For six decades, rockets were single-use: every launch meant building a new rocket, which is why spaceflight cost hundreds of millions per flight. Reusability is the change that made satellite constellations and routine launches economically possible.

exploreAction.targetName: The 21 December 2015 booster landing + the cost-reduction math
exploreAction.instruction: Read the 2015 landing's history and the failures before it: the first landing attempts exploded at sea, and the company was nearly bankrupt in 2008 — the reusable rocket was a decade-long bet that looked reckless for years.

name: Telomerase (1984)
teaser: Telomerase — the enzyme that lengthens the protective caps (telomeres) on chromosome ends — was discovered in 1984 by Elizabeth Blackburn and Carol Greider, who shared the 2009 Nobel with Jack Szostak. It's the molecule that lets some cells divide forever: active in stem cells and embryos, hijacked by cancers, and absent in most adult cells, which is why our chromosomes shorten as we age.

exploreAction.targetName: The 1984 telomerase discovery + its role in cancer
exploreAction.instruction: Read the discovery story and notice the unlikely setting: Greider was a graduate student who ran the experiments over a Christmas holiday, looking for an enzyme that lengthens the six-base repeating 'TTAGGG' sequence at chromosome tips. Then read the two-faced biology: telomerase keeps germ cells and stem cells young, but ~90% of cancers activate it too — which is why the enzyme is simultaneously a longevity lead and a cancer target.

name: The Cell Cycle (2001)
teaser: The discovery of the cell cycle's molecular clock — the cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases that decide when a cell divides — won the 2001 Nobel for Leland Hartwell, Tim Hunt, and Paul Nurse. The machinery they found is so universal that the yeast they studied and human cells run on the same proteins, which is why the cell-cycle research became the foundation of cancer biology.

exploreAction.targetName: The 2001 Nobel work — cyclins, CDKs, and checkpoints
